projects.title: PCA-Based Subspace Analysis of Motor-Imagination EEG Signals
projects.summary: In this project, I looked at whether different motor-imagery EEG conditions actually produce distinct principal component subspaces using PCA on the PhysioNet EEG Motor Movement/Imagery dataset. More specifically, I wanted to understand whether the structure of the EEG signals themselves changes in a meaningful way across conditions like left fist, right fist, both fists, both feet, and rest, or whether the dominant structure of the feature space instead stays mostly the same across those conditions. After comparing these condition-specific subspaces across 106 subjects and 64 EEG channels, I found that the principal angles between the condition subspaces remained very small, around 4° to 6°, which seems to suggest that most of the large-scale variance captured by PCA is likely reflecting subject-specific neural structure rather than clear separation between the motor-task conditions themselves. Because of this, it seems reasonable to think that broadband PCA alone is probably not capturing strong condition-level structure in the EEG signals at the level of these dominant principal subspaces.
projects.description:
The pipeline begins by extracting event-centered EEG epochs from the PhysioNet Motor Movement/Imagery dataset and then converting each epoch into a 64-dimensional spatial feature representation by averaging activity across time within each EEG channel. I noticed that this step reduces the dimensionality of the feature space while still preserving the spatial structure of the EEG signals across the scalp, which helps make the PCA analysis more interpretable in practice. After applying z-score normalization across channels, I then performed PCA separately for each movement condition, and when looking at the cumulative explained variance across components, I found that only a relatively small number of components were needed to capture most of the signal energy in the feature space itself.

To test whether these different motor tasks actually produced distinct neural subspaces, I computed principal angles between the condition-specific PCA bases. When looking at these subspace comparisons themselves, I noticed that the condition subspaces remained strongly aligned across all condition pairs, especially when compared to the random-subspace baseline. Because of this consistent alignment across the condition subspaces, it seems to suggest that broadband PCA is mostly capturing subject-level structure rather than condition-level structure across these movement tasks.

Another important thing I examined was reconstruction-error behavior using truncated singular value decomposition. When I looked at how much signal energy remained after removing the top principal components, I found that a single principal component alone appeared to account for roughly 82% to 85% of the signal energy across all conditions. This kind of pattern seems to suggest that the EEG feature space itself has a strong low-rank structure overall, which helps explain why PCA-based signal compression and the resulting artifact removal can be useful as a preprocessing step in EEG analysis workflows.

I also performed frequency-band PCA within the theta, alpha, and beta ranges, because I wanted to check whether condition-related structure might appear more clearly inside these particular frequency bands rather than in the broadband EEG signals themselves. What stood out to me here was that the beta band appeared to show clearer condition-related organization compared to the theta band, which seems consistent with what is already known about motor-related beta desynchronization near sensorimotor cortex. Because of this frequency-band structure, it seems reasonable to think that band-limited PCA representations may help support how movement-related neural activity is interpreted in practice, especially in contexts like brain–computer interface systems or clinical EEG monitoring workflows.

Overall, I believe this process suggests that PCA-based subspace comparisons are probably more useful for understanding the subject-level structure of the EEG signals and the dimensionality of the feature space itself than for directly separating movement conditions using broadband EEG representations alone.
